SM18L-A1.free_elimination: -12 is the printed 12 with a sign flip (echo); -3/-2 form the only adjacent pair but that cuts neither way
SM18L-A1.note: Standard 'same slope so must coincide' item; 'at least one solution' wording is the only twist. Ratio 4:-6 = 2:3 reused verbatim in B3.

SM18L-A2.free_elimination: 48 dies to a range bound read off y<=-x+27 with y>=0 (x<=27), no arithmetic; 15 is the intersection's y-coordinate but that needs the solve
SM18L-A2.note: One vertex computation; 'quadrilateral' hands the student the shape. Real m2-hard would ask for a max of an objective, not a coordinate.

SM18L-A3.free_elimination: 12 = 4*3, product of two printed numbers (closure); 45 = 15*3 also a printed product but reads as the table difference times 3 and needs the table read
SM18L-A3.note: Composed slope. Routine route (f=3x+5, g=12t+2, subtract) reaches 36 with no insight; the intended 'intercept cancels' is nice but not required.

SM18L-A4.free_elimination: 12 = 2*6 (doubled printed number, closure); 21 = 15+6 needs c. Also a magnitude tell: |3x-c|<=6 pins x to a band of width 12/3 without touching the midpoint
SM18L-A4.note: Midpoint is a red herring, which is the only decision point; a student who just finds c=15 and solves 3<=x<=7 gets 4 routinely. Key is the smallest option.

SM18L-A5.free_elimination: none clean: all four sit under 180 and none is a printed product; 176 = 180-4 and 168 = 180-12 both need the model
SM18L-A5.note: Decision point (min is on pages, max is on cost; is 180 attainable at integer pages) is real but small. p=420 attains 180 exactly, so 'greatest possible cost' is well-defined. Second-cleanest item in the A run.

SM18L-A6.free_elimination: none; 21 = 3*7 is a printed-times-key product but a student cannot see that without the key
SM18L-A6.note: Match the y-coefficient. One rearrangement plus one equation; c = 10.5 is a non-integer, which is fine since it is not asked. Key is the smallest option.

SM18L-A7.free_elimination: 4 is printed in a denominator, so it is dead before any algebra (that is the intended trap, but it is also a free strike for a careful reader). No other free kill.
SM18L-A7.note: Extraneous root as the decision point; the quadratic's other root IS the excluded value, so a student who skips the check lands on the trap. Verification in the explanation (42/187 both sides) is correct. Borderline for Algebra vs Advanced Math (quadratic appears), but rational equations in one variable are on the SAT Algebra list. Key is the smallest option.

SM18L-B1.free_elimination: 74 requires 1 sq yd = 1 sq ft; since a yard is longer than a foot the cost must exceed 60+0.35*40 strictly, so 74 dies on a magnitude read. 126 < 60+anything plausible? no, 126 survives.
SM18L-B1.note: A unit-conversion item with a square trap. Not a module-2 hard construct; it is a medium at best on the real test and the whole item is the procedure. Key is the LARGEST option, the only one in the batch.

SM18L-B2.free_elimination: none clean. 49 = 7^2 but 7 is not printed; 29 needs x,y.
SM18L-B2.note: Classic symmetric-system sum/difference. Brute force (x=5,y=2) reaches 21 in four lines, so the factoring insight is optional. A frequently seen prep item.

SM18L-B3.free_elimination: none; k=2 would zero the run but 2 is not an option. -8 is the only negative but a negative k is not obviously illegal.
SM18L-B3.note: Slope of 4x-6y=7 is 2/3, same coefficient pair and same ratio as A1. One linear equation in k after the slope is set. Key is 2nd-largest.

SM18L-B4.free_elimination: none without computing the $78 boundary; once that one product is done 420 dies, but that is arithmetic.
SM18L-B4.note: Tiered pricing, locate tier, back out. Purely procedural; the 'decision' (which tier) is one comparison. Distractor derivations all check.

SM18L-B5.free_elimination: none. Recounted: x<-3 gives -12..-4 = 9; x>8 gives 9..12 = 4; total 13. The bounds -12..12 admit at most 24 (x=-3 excluded), so 19 is not out of range.
SM18L-B5.note: Genuine decision point: naive cross-multiplication yields x>8 and the distractor 4. All three distractor derivations verified (19 = integers <8 minus -3 = 20-1; 10 = -2..7). Best item in the batch. Key 2nd-largest.

SM18L-B6.note: Recounted: x = 4 + 30/(k-3); positive divisors of 30 = 8 (all x>0); negative d with 30/d > -4 => d in {-10,-15,-30} = 3; k=3 gives x=-6. 11 correct, and the 13-distractor (8+5 wrong-sign negatives) checks. But counting integer divisors of a constant for which an equation has a positive-integer solution is competition number theory, not a Digital SAT Algebra construct; the SAT never asks 'for how many integer k'. Hard, but off-blueprint. Key 2nd-largest.

SM18L-B7.free_elimination: none clean; a=-3 (dependent case) is not offered, 2 is the x-value echo but only after solving.
SM18L-B7.note: Solve a 2x2 without the parameter, substitute once. 'Exactly one solution' clause is decoration (only a=-3 would break it). This is a module-1 item. Key 2nd-largest.
